summary: China's factories shrank again in October as shoppers held back, while BYD's best month of the year came mostly from sales abroad.
body: China's official factory survey fell to 49.3 in October, below the 50 line that separates growth from shrinking, for the third time in four months [^1]. Services and construction also slipped [^1]. An official at the group that runs the survey said "insufficient demand" is adding pressure, and spending faded after the October National Day holiday [^1]. The split is sharp: makers of AI hardware, trains and aircraft did well, while firms tied to housing struggled [^1]. Growth for the year is still expected to reach the 4.5-5% target [^1].

Electric cars show where growth is coming from. BYD, the largest EV maker, sold about 490,000 vehicles in October, its best month this year, and more than 300,000 fully electric cars for the first time [^2]. About a third of its sales were overseas, double a year earlier, while its total sales for the year are slightly down [^2]. Rivals Leapmotor and Xiaomi also posted strong months [^3].

Daily life reflects careful spending. Youth unemployment (ages 16-24, not in school) eased to 18% in September but was the highest September figure since this series began in 2024 [^5]. Shops are working hard for those customers: Alibaba expects a record 1 million brands in its Singles Day festival, which peaks on Nov 11, with an AI assistant to compare products [^4]. On technology, Beijing's proposed export controls on AI models and chips are open for comment until Nov 15 [^6]. The Register reports, citing Chinese state media, that DeepSeek has been allowed to keep exporting [^7].
differences: Reports differ on how far the AI export rules go: The National describes proposed rules open for comment until Nov 15, while The Register describes restrictions already in place with licences required [^6][^7]. BYD's October total is about 490,000 vehicles in CnEVPost and 483,125 passenger cars in CarNewsChina; the gap is likely commercial vehicles [^2][^3].

reads.summary: Ten ordinary people, from an 11-year-old making songs to a 79-year-old with an AI companion, on how AI has entered daily life in China.
